stances.claim: Andy Bautista is virtually immune from criminal prosecution under the Anti-Graft Law and Anti-Money Laundering Act, and from disbarment, while he remains Comelec chair — because any penalty including removal/disqualification from public office can only be imposed through impeachment, not through criminal or administrative proceedings.
stances.rhetorical_move: constitutional-immunity application: Comelec chair's bar membership requirement creates an automatic disqualification trigger that collapses criminal and disbarment proceedings into the impeachment-exclusive channel

stances.claim: Patricia Bautista faces a spousal disqualification bar under Rule 130 Sec. 22 — she cannot testify for or against Andy in impeachment proceedings — because impeachment is sui generis (neither civil nor criminal) and is not a case by one spouse against the other.
stances.rhetorical_move: procedural-classification argument: the sui generis nature of impeachment places it outside both exceptions to the spousal privilege
stances.confidence: asserted as probable legal outcome, left open as question for follow-up

stances.claim: Andy Bautista may have inadvertently waived his spousal privilege and effectively consented to Tish's testimony by filing criminal cases (robbery, extortion) against her — an unresolved legal conundrum that the column flags for future analysis.
stances.rhetorical_move: waiver-by-conduct hypothesis — filing suit against spouse as implied consent to spouse's adverse testimony
stances.confidence: posed as open question ('did Andy effectively waive…?')

notable_anecdotes: The full media circus framing in the opening — Tish's affidavit becoming 'fodder of TV, radio and newspaper interviews by the couple themselves, their lawyers and relatives,' opening 'their private lives to ugly rumors, unfair social media trolls and salacious coffee talk' — before CJ pivots to public-interest analysis only, modeling disciplined legal commentary over tabloid engagement.

The constitutional twist: because the 1987 Constitution requires the Comelec chair to be a member of the Philippine bar, any criminal indictment or disbarment order would automatically oust him from a constitutionally-defined office — which can only happen through impeachment, creating an ironclad immunity that most commentators missed.

The spousal-privilege paradox: Andy's own decision to file criminal cases against Tish — for robbery and extortion — could be read as waiving his right to block her testimony, meaning his legal counter-offensive may have undermined his own privilege defense; CJ flags this and defers resolution to a follow-up column.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban uses the Bautista marital scandal -- Patricia 'Tish' Bautista's August 1, 2017 affidavit alleging her husband Comelec Chair Andy Bautista's violations of the Anti-Graft Law, Anti-Money Laundering Act, SALN obligations, and professional ethics -- to analyze three distinct legal conundrums while deliberately sidestepping the tabloid dimensions. First, he establishes that Andy is virtually immune from criminal prosecution and disbarment while in office: because the Constitution requires the Comelec chair to be a bar member, any criminal penalty or disbarment order would automatically oust him from a constitutionally-defined position, and such ouster can only be accomplished through impeachment -- meaning indictments must wait until he leaves office. Second, he examines whether Tish can testify against Andy in impeachment proceedings under Rule 130 Sec. 22's spousal disqualification rule, arguing that since impeachment is sui generis (neither civil nor criminal) and is not a case by one spouse against the other, the rule's exceptions do not apply and she faces a testimonial bar. Third, he raises -- but does not resolve -- whether Andy's filing of criminal cases (robbery, extortion) against Tish constitutes an implied waiver of his spousal privilege and consent to her adverse testimony, promising further analysis in a follow-up column.
